name: Aaron Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent of AI companies, employers, unions, political parties and government, and we sell nothing or campaign for any side. Your answers stay confidential and your name won't be attached. What does an ordinary day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the pharmacy delivery complaints team at a contact centre. A patient rings because a parcel of medicine was left on the wrong doorstep, and I trace the delivery record and call the driver before I authorise a replacement. My two-year college diploma helped me into office work, but fifteen years on these calls taught me the delicate part.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the delicate part, and what is home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The patient may be scared or angry, and my team has to be accurate without making them repeat the story. I use approved AI search every day to find a policy, then check the actual delivery record. My partner Leila works at a community hall, our grown children rent elsewhere, and we have four months of expenses saved on two ordinary wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team a small shortcut is fine if we keep the time to call the driver and the patient. I would say the delivery record, not a tidy paragraph, decides where a medicine parcel went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect these complaints to keep arriving, and my lead wage should hold. Four months saved means Leila and I can handle an ordinary repair without borrowing, though I would watch management's call-time target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would keep checking delivery records before approving replacements and use the approved search as I already do. In the first year of AI Plateau I would take three wrong delivery summaries to the team meeting and ask with the other leads that correction time stay in the paid target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the work and money for now. I get cross when a speed measure treats a second call as a fresh surprise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened with a wrong delivery summary?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last Tuesday a summary said delivered, but the driver had photographed the neighbouring porch. The patient needed a new parcel, and the team needed time to correct the address.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the reserve for anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leila and I would keep the four-month reserve for repairs and bills, not use it to reward a small software saving. The children have their own rent and should not be our fallback.

I would ask for **paid correction time** with the other leads.
think: I expect my **lead wage** to hold through modest change.
I watch **call-time targets** despite a four-month household reserve.
do: Keep checking **delivery records** before replacements and use approved search as before.
Bring **three wrong summaries** to the team meeting and ask with leads for paid correction time.
feel: I feel **calm** about wages, while impatient with speed-only targets.

fieldNote: He uses approved **AI search daily** but checks the delivery record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the floor that easy delivery questions may go to software, but a wrong medicine address needs a paid person to fix it. I would ask our staff association to demand weekly appeal hours alongside the new bot statistics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My team may keep difficult complaints, but it might be half as large. I could lose paid lead hours even if management still calls me a lead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would test the new AI address checker on twenty closed misdeliveries during paid time if my supervisor approves error logging. In the first year routine chats move, I would join the association's written request for paid appeal hours and keep the offered human complaints shifts while comparing the new rota with our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a smaller paid week, interested in whether the checker actually gets the house right. A patient cannot take a replacement label as medicine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you count as a repeat call?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count a repeat call when the patient says the same parcel still has not arrived. That is a second piece of paid work even if the bot closed the first ticket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would two lost days mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the team drops two paid days, Leila and I can draw on the reserve for a short period, but we would not call it a permanent wage. I would ask management for a written timetable before spending that buffer.

I cannot treat **four months saved** as permanent replacement pay.

If two paid days go, use our **four-month reserve** briefly and ask management for a written timetable before spending it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues thinking AI by 2028 could settle most delivery claims before the driver even returns to the depot. Hands-on robots arrive around 2031, but our desk has the earlier problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of my team's paid hours could end before the association wins a new rota. Four months saved and Leila's hall wage give us some search time, not enough to assume we can stop earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would join the association's request for written notice and final paid-shift dates, then list monthly bills with Leila. If most lead hours end in the first year after 2028, I would apply for posted paid pharmacy-counter work nearby and accept only written full-week wages and hours covering our bills after travel; I would keep any paid complaints shifts still offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed at the speed and the possibility that most of my wage goes. I can make calls to employers, but I cannot create a counter opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check at the pharmacy counter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether that counter actually has paid staff helping patients with missing orders. A volunteer place or a single Sunday shift would not replace our weekly bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children fund a gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children could listen while we read an advert, but I would not ask them to fund our rent. Leila and I would use our savings for a search only if the hours really ended.

I would ask for **written final shifts** through our association.
think: I expect **most paid lead hours** might end quickly.
I cannot rely on **four months saved** as lasting household income.
do: Join a **shared notice request** and list bills with Leila in 2026.
After most **2028 hours end**, apply for posted pharmacy work; accept only written after-travel weekly wages and hours covering bills.
feel: I feel **alarmed** at the likely loss of most paid hours.
S2.quote: I can make calls to employers, but I cannot create a counter opening.
fieldNote: He treats a **posted paid opening** as necessary, with no invented training route.
He keeps **available paid shifts** during the search and checks full-week after-travel affordability before accepting another job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to check whether the specialist queue is actually kept, if workers get the figures. Thinking AI reaches claims by 2031; capable delivery robots would follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may keep hard medicine complaints while the simple queue thins, but that does not promise me full lead hours. I could be 63 by then, and I do not know what income would let Leila and me reduce work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would propose a quarterly association check of paid appeal hours beside the number of medicines delivered to wrong addresses. I would keep handling paid complaints and save a small extra amount in months the hall gives Leila full hours; if my own shifts fall after 2031, I would inspect posted local patient-service work before making an application.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though the slower date gives us a way to make the employer show its sums. I would rather negotiate from a real count than from a promise on a poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you count a genuine appeal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count an appeal only when the patient still lacks the right medicine after the first answer. The raw number of chatbot replies would tell us nothing about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you reduce work at 63?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I cannot call 63 a retirement date. We need actual income statements and a year of bills before either of us gives up paid shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team a decade is enough to make a proper record of paid appeals and household bills, if we start while wages arrive. Thinking AI reaches medicine claims around 2036, and delivery robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may want fewer late calls, but I cannot name what would replace the wage. Four months saved is helpful for a gap; it is not an income for the years after work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter Leila and I would gather actual income statements and write down a full year of bills. I would keep paid complaint shifts and ask the association to publish annual paid appeal hours; after 2036, I would only reduce paid work if our verified income covers bills and keep looking at actual offered shifts if it does not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the distant desk changes, but the household is steady today. I would rather check the figures than declare retirement on a calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you count the hall wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count the hall's quieter months as well as its busy bookings. An average wage made from the best months alone is not a household budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children help later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children can choose their own lives, and I would not ask them to finance ours. If we have a later shortfall, Leila and I must first see what paid work and verified income actually exist.

I would say **2036 claims AI** comes before 2039 delivery robots.

If verified income falls short after 2036, check **actually offered paid shifts** before changing work.

fieldNote: He checks **hall income variability** and refuses to call savings retirement pay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 version, because the team could lose most of its wage before the pharmacy opens another paid seat. Written human-appeal hours and a real local vacancy would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how many wrong medicine deliveries are actually put right, not just how quickly a chatbot closes them. The parcel has to reach the patient.

headlineQuote: The parcel has to reach the patient.
portrait: A **58-year-old** pharmacy-delivery complaints lead with a two-year college diploma and strong skill.
He uses **approved AI daily**, checking each search against the delivery record.
Leila's **community-hall wage** and four months saved allow some planning, while he keeps paid work central.
He pushes for **shared appeal-hour figures** and refuses to assume retirement income or child support.
biggestWorry: The **2028 AGI** picture could end most lead hours before another paid pharmacy seat exists.
whatWouldHelp: Written **human-appeal hours** and a genuine local paid vacancy would help.
